msg: SPF record needs {n} DNS lookups — the limit is 10. Receivers return PermError and treat the domain as having no SPF at all. Flatten or remove includes. [RFC 7208 4.6.4, IETF, April 2014]

SPF record already spends {n} of the 10 permitted DNS lookups in the record itself; every include: resolves to a record that can spend more. Count the nested ones before you publish. [RFC 7208 4.6.4, IETF, April 2014]
'+all' (or a bare 'all') passes SPF for every sender on the internet, which is the same as publishing no SPF. End the record with '-all', or '~all' while you migrate. [RFC 7208 5.1, IETF, April 2014]

The 'ptr' mechanism is deprecated and must not be published — receivers may ignore it, and it costs a DNS lookup per candidate host. Replace it with ip4:/ip6: or include:. [RFC 7208 5.5, IETF, April 2014: 'its use is discouraged']

SPF record has no 'all' mechanism and no 'redirect=' modifier, so everything it does not list gets Neutral — the same result as no policy. Add '-all' or '~all' at the end. [RFC 7208 4.7, IETF, April 2014]
Second 'v=spf1' record published on the same name. More than one SPF record for a domain is a PermError — merge them into one record. [RFC 7208 4.5, IETF, April 2014]

A single quoted TXT string is {n} characters; the DNS wire format caps one character-string at 255. Split it into several quoted strings on the same record — they are concatenated with no separator. [RFC 1035 3.3.14, IETF, November 1987]

DMARC record has no 'p=' tag. Under DMARCbis this no longer voids the record — it is now read as 'p=none', so the domain looks protected in an audit and blocks nothing. Publish 'p=' explicitly. [RFC 9989 4.7, IETF, May 2026: 'If this tag is not present in an otherwise syntactically valid DMARC Policy Record, then the record is treated as if it included p=none' — this REPLACES the RFC 7489 behaviour of discarding the record]

'p=none' only asks for reports; receivers still deliver mail that fails alignment, so nothing is blocked. It satisfies 'a DMARC record exists' and nothing else — move to quarantine, then reject. [RFC 9989 4.7, IETF, May 2026]

'pct={n}' was removed from DMARC in May 2026. A receiver following the current spec ignores it, so a record you published as a {n}% staged rollout now applies your full policy to 100% of your mail. Delete 'pct=' and stage with 't=y' instead. [RFC 9989 Appendix A.6 'Removal of the pct tag', IETF, 21 May 2026]

't=y' is DMARC test mode: receivers apply the policy one level below the one you published, so 'p=reject' behaves as quarantine and 'p=quarantine' as none. Correct while you stage a rollout, silent failure if it is left on. [RFC 9989 4.7, IETF, May 2026: 'the policy applied to any failing messages will be one level below the specified policy']

'np=none' switches off the policy for subdomains that do not exist — the names a spoofer picks precisely because nobody has claimed them. Set 'np=reject', or drop the tag so the domain policy is inherited. [RFC 9989 4.7, IETF, May 2026: np = policy 'for non-existent subdomains of the Organizational Domain queried']

No 'rua=' tag, so no aggregate reports are ever sent: you cannot see which of your senders fail alignment, and you hold no evidence that the policy was enforced on any given date. Add rua=mailto: before you tighten the policy. [RFC 9990 3.4, IETF, May 2026: 'The presence of the rua tag specifies where to send feedback']

'rua=' sends aggregate reports to {n}, which is outside this domain. That destination must publish an authorisation record before any receiver will send to it; without it the reports are silently dropped and your evidence trail is empty. [RFC 9990 4, IETF, May 2026: verification requires a TXT record at '_report._dmarc' prepended to the reporting destination, e.g. yourdomain._report._dmarc.<destination>]

A DMARC record is only read at the name '_dmarc.<domain>'. This record is published somewhere else, so no receiver will ever look it up. [RFC 9989 4.5, IETF, May 2026: policy records are published at '_dmarc prepended to domain name']

'sp=none' overrides the policy for every subdomain, so mail from a subdomain nobody uses is unprotected while the parent domain is enforced. Drop 'sp=' to inherit, or set sp=reject. [RFC 9989 4.7, IETF, May 2026 — note the organizational domain is now found by the DNS Tree Walk (4.10), not the public suffix list]

Empty 'p=' in a DKIM record means the key is revoked — every signature made with this selector fails, and mail signed only by it loses DKIM. Publish the public key or delete the selector. [RFC 6376 3.6.1, IETF, September 2011]

The 'p=' key blob is {n} base64 characters, which is about a 1024-bit RSA key or smaller. Signers must use at least 1024 bits and should use 2048 — rotate the selector. [RFC 8301 3.2, IETF, January 2018]
't=y' puts the selector in test mode, which tells receivers to treat a failed signature as if the message were unsigned. Remove it once the selector is live. [RFC 6376 3.6.1, IETF, September 2011]
